query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the tendency to form and retain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the nature of element X; if X (Al or Si) forms an oxide with a crystal structure and thermal expansion closely matching that of the metallic matrix, the resulting scale relieves interfacial stresses and remains adherent, whereas if X is Mn, the oxide formed is less coherent and prone to cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, where X is either Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (above 900 °C) exposure in air or a controlled oxidative/corrosive environment; comparisons are made among alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent oxide scale that matches the underlying alloy in crystallography and thermal expansion.
generation.mechanism: Element X reacts with oxygen to form an oxide. For alloys with X = Al or Si, the resulting oxide has structural compatibility (i.e., similar lattice parameters and low thermal expansion mismatch) with the substrate, reducing growth-induced stresses and minimizing spallation; for X = Mn, the oxide formed lacks these favorable attributes and becomes unstable under thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will form a slow-growing, continuous and coherent oxide layer that persists under high temperature, while alloys with X = Mn will develop less adherent, unstable oxide scales that crack or spall.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNiMn alloy, where the absence of a strongly reactive element that forms a structurally compatible oxide leads to unstable oxide scale formation under the same exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in solid-solution states subjected to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; effects outside these conditions are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise degree of matching in thermal expansion and crystallography between the oxide and the substrate, as well as the kinetics of oxide formation, may vary with slight compositional changes and phase distributions, making quantitative predictions of oxide thickness or lifetime uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Al, Si, and Mn in similar solid-solution states. Anneal all samples at temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative atmosphere for a fixed time period. Analyze the surface oxide scales for morphology, phase continuity, adhesion, and spallation behavior.
measurements: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to assess oxide morphology and spallation
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) or X-ray diffraction (XRD) to evaluate crystallographic coherence between the oxide and substrate
Adhesion tests to quantitatively measure the strength of the oxide scale attachment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if alloys with X = Al or Si do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide layer coherence and adhesion compared to the Mn-containing alloy, or if the Mn-containing alloy forms an oxide scale that performs equivalently in terms of stability under the same high-temperature exposure.

Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film

Abstract: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys

Abstract: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Spinel-Type (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4 High-Entropy Oxide: Facile Preparation and Supercapacitor Performance

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have attracted more and more attention because of their unique structures and potential applications. In this work, (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4 HEO powders were synthesized via a facile solid-state reaction route. The confirmation of phase composition, the observation of microstructure, and the analysis of crystal structure, distribution of elements, and valences of elements were conducted by X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), respectively. Furthermore, a (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4/nickel foam ((FeCoCrMnZn)3O4/NF) electrode was prepared via a coating method, followed by the investigation of its supercapacitor performance. The results show that, after calcining (FeCoCrMnZn)3O4 powders at 900 °C for 2 h, a single spinel structure (FCC, Fd-3m, a = 0.8399 nm) was obtained with uniform distribution of Fe, Co, Cr, Mn, and Zn elements, the typical characteristic of a high-entropy oxide.
